This vignette demonstrates a complete example of how to use the `Entropy` package to compute entropy values for cells in a Seurat object.

## Load libraries and data

```{r}
library(Entropy)
library(Seurat)

data("pbmc_small")
DefaultAssay(pbmc_small) <- "RNA"
```

## Run entropy in counts mode

```{r}
result_counts <- run_entropy(
  seu = pbmc_small,
  assay = "RNA",
  neighbors = NULL,
  neighbors_method = "auto",
  output_path = NULL,
  add_assay = TRUE,
  mode = "counts"
)
```

## Inspect entropy assay

```{r}
result_counts[["RNA_entropy"]]
```

## Visualize entropy distribution

```{r}
means_counts <- colMeans(GetAssayData(result_counts[["RNA_entropy"]], layer = "counts"))

hist(
  means_counts,
  main = "Counts entropy distribution",
  xlab = "Mean entropy",
  col = "steelblue"
)
```

## Run entropy in binary mode

Binary mode binarizes the count matrix (`counts > 0`) and computes Shannon entropy.

```{r}
result_binary <- run_entropy(
  seu = pbmc_small,
  assay = "RNA",
  neighbors = NULL,
  neighbors_method = "auto",
  output_path = NULL,
  add_assay = FALSE,
  mode = "binary"
)
```

## Inspect binary entropy output

```{r}
head(result_binary)
```

## Visualize binary entropy distribution

```{r}
hist(
  result_binary[[1]],
  main = "Binary entropy distribution",
  xlab = "Mean entropy",
  col = "darkorange"
)
```

## Run entropy restricted within groups

The `restrict_by` argument restricts each cell's neighbors to cells sharing the
same value in a metadata column, so entropy is computed *within* groups rather
than across them. Here we use the `groups` column of `pbmc_small`.

```{r}
result_restricted <- run_entropy(
  seu = pbmc_small,
  assay = "RNA",
  neighbors_method = "auto",
  add_assay = FALSE,
  mode = "counts",
  restrict_by = "groups"
)
```

## Compare unrestricted vs restricted

```{r}
means_restricted <- result_restricted[[1]]

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
hist(means_counts, main = "Unrestricted", xlab = "Mean entropy",
     col = "steelblue", xlim = range(c(means_counts, means_restricted)))
hist(means_restricted, main = "Restricted within groups", xlab = "Mean entropy",
     col = "seagreen", xlim = range(c(means_counts, means_restricted)))
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

Restricting neighbors to within-group cells changes each cell's neighborhood
composition, which shifts the entropy estimates. On a small demonstration
dataset like `pbmc_small` the magnitude of the difference is not biologically
meaningful — the purpose here is to show the effect of the `restrict_by`
argument on the computation, not to interpret the values.


## Score gene sets with `add_entropy_score`

Once entropy has been computed and stored as an assay (`add_assay = TRUE`), the
`add_entropy_score()` function can quickly summarise the mean entropy of one or
more gene sets and add each as a metadata column. It does not recompute
anything, it simply averages the already stored per-gene entropy, so it is a
fast way to score many pathways or regulons at once.

We pass a named list of gene sets. Each name becomes a metadata column prefixed
with `entropy_` (for example `Tcell` becomes `entropy_Tcell`). Here we use
`force_drop = TRUE` so that any gene not present in the entropy assay is dropped
with a warning rather than raising an error.

```{r}
gene_sets <- list(
  Tcell = c("CD3D", "CD3E", "CD8A", "IL7R"),
  Bcell = c("CD79A", "CD79B", "MS4A1")
)

result_counts <- add_entropy_score(
  seu           = result_counts,
  entropy_assay = "RNA_entropy",
  features_list = gene_sets,
  force_drop    = TRUE
)

head(result_counts[[c("entropy_Tcell", "entropy_Bcell")]])
```

## Visualise gene set entropy

Because the scores are stored in the metadata, they can be visualised directly
with Seurat's `FeaturePlot` on any existing reduction. `pbmc_small` ships with a
t-SNE embedding, so we use that.

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.5}
FeaturePlot(
  result_counts,
  features  = c("entropy_Tcell", "entropy_Bcell"),
  reduction = "tsne"
)
```

Each cell is coloured by the mean entropy of the corresponding gene set, giving
a per-cell view of how variable those genes are within each cell's
neighbourhood. On a small demonstration dataset the values are mainly
illustrative, but on a full dataset this is a quick way to compare the entropy
of different pathways or regulons across cell populations.
